title: bf16 Rounding Silently Discards Most RL Policy Updates: A Hidden Training-Inference Mismatch and an Unbiased One-Line Fix
content:
Computer Science > Machine Learning
  [Submitted on 29 Oct 2026]
Title:bf16 Rounding Silently Discards Most RL Policy Updates: A Hidden Training-Inference Mismatch and an Unbiased One-Line Fix
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of language models keeps fp32 master weights in the optimizer and serves rollouts from a bf16 copy produced by round-to-nearest conversion. At the learning rates in common use, most per-step updates are smaller than half a bf16 spacing and the conversion discards them: on Qwen3-1.7B only 0.4-0.5% of served weights change per step, and the policy that generates the training data lags the optimizer by 50-150 steps. Existing mismatch corrections cannot see this lag because they compare two copies downstream of the same rounding. We propose Fair Cast: export the master with an unbiased rounding rule (stochastic rounding or error feedback) and compute the training loss on the served copy. The change is one line at the export call, adds no hyperparameters and costs 22-38 ms per export of 1.7B parameters. Across 25 matched seed-pairs on Qwen3-0.6B to 4B with AdamW and Muon, Fair Cast is ahead on 18, tied on 6 and behind on 1, with a mean gain of 6.1 points; on zebra puzzles it reaches 0.57 +/- 0.16 over four runs where round-to-nearest collapses to 0.33 +/- 0.10. It also makes the saved fp32 checkpoint agree with the served model, and it exposes the implicit lag of round-to-nearest as a regularizer that can be restored explicitly when a task needs it.

report.summary: Round-to-nearest bf16 export silently discards most RL weight updates in LLM post-training; a one-line unbiased-rounding fix restores them, gaining ~6 points on average.
report.background: Modern RL post-training (RLHF/RLVR pipelines built on PPO, GRPO and similar algorithms) keeps a high-precision fp32 copy of the model in the optimizer, but rollout generation runs on a bf16 copy pushed to an inference engine such as vLLM or SGLang. bf16 has only 8 explicit mantissa bits, so its relative spacing is roughly 0.4%. At the learning rates commonly used, a single gradient step moves a weight by far less than half of that spacing, so the round-to-nearest export snaps the weight back to its previous value. The optimizer 'learns' while the policy that actually generates training data stays frozen. This is a distinct, previously unmeasured member of the training-inference mismatch family, alongside MoE routing drift, KV-cache precision and logits discrepancies that importance-sampling corrections like truncated importance sampling were designed to address. Because those corrections compare two tensors that have both already passed through the same rounding step, they are structurally blind to this particular lag.
key_points: Round-to-nearest bf16 export throws away most updates. On Qwen3-1.7B only 0.4-0.5% of served weights change per optimizer step, so the policy generating rollouts trails the optimizer by roughly 50-150 steps, effectively training on stale data.

Existing mismatch corrections cannot see the problem. Importance-sampling and ratio-based fixes compare two copies that sit downstream of the same bf16 rounding, so the divergence between the fp32 master weights and the served model is invisible to them.

The proposed fix, 'Fair Cast', is one line at the export call. Instead of round-to-nearest, export with stochastic rounding or error feedback, and compute the training loss on the served copy. No new hyperparameters; 22-38 ms per 1.7B-parameter export.

It wins empirically. Across 25 matched seed-pairs on Qwen3-0.6B to 4B with both AdamW and Muon, Fair Cast is ahead on 18, tied on 6 and behind on 1, with a mean gain of 6.1 points; on zebra puzzles it scores 0.57 +/- 0.16 versus 0.33 +/- 0.10.

Two side benefits. The saved fp32 checkpoint now agrees with what is actually served, removing a silent checkpoint/serving discrepancy, and the lag inherent to round-to-nearest is reframed as an implicit regularizer that can be reintroduced deliberately when a task benefits from it.
report.impact: For the AI industry this is a cheap, high-leverage correction to a bug hiding in plain sight across nearly every RL post-training stack: clusters are spending GPU hours on updates that a 16-bit cast quietly erases, and the effect worsens at the small learning rates typically used for stable RL fine-tuning. Teams running verl, OpenRLHF, TRL or in-house GRPO loops should audit their export path immediately, since the patch is a single call site rather than an architectural change. For developers, the lesson is that 'the training loss went down' is not evidence the served policy improved; logging the fraction of weights that actually changed between steps is a cheap new diagnostic. It also strengthens the case for computing loss on exactly the tensor that was served. For regular users, the practical payoff is stronger reasoning behaviour from the same compute budget, and fewer of the subtle regressions that plague RL-finetuned models.
report.tools: Watch the paper's arXiv page (2610.41073) and the alphaXiv discussion for reference implementations. To try it, patch the weight-export call in your RL stack: verl, OpenRLHF or HuggingFace TRL for training, with vLLM or SGLang on the serving side. Look for stochastic-rounding or error-feedback CUDA kernels in PyTorch, JAX and torchao, and add a simple monitor that logs the L2 norm of the delta between fp32 master weights and the bf16 served copy each step to confirm updates are surviving the cast.
